procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge, Pune under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed Criminal Bail Application No. 3007 of 2021 in the High Court of Judicature at Bombay on 27th October 2018, appealing the Special Judge's decision. The High Court rejected their prayers for bail on 15th October 2019.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court challenging the judgments of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay that rejected their bail applications. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgments, and directed that the appellants be released on bail, subject to terms and conditions set by the Special Court.

directions: Appellants be released on bail, on such terms and conditions the Special Court may consider fit.

issue.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of granting bail, the court is required to form a prima facie opinion based on the materials on record that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty, with such findings being tentative and not influencing the trial on merits.

law.fact_text: A statutory provision (proviso) dictates that an accused person shall not be released on bail if the court, after reviewing the case diary or police report (under Section 173 CrPC), is of the opinion that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accusation against them is 'prima facie true'.
The court's duty is to form an opinion based on these materials to determine if the accusation is prima facie true. This is a prerequisite for rejecting a bail application.
While a detailed examination of evidence and merits is not required at the bail stage, the court must still provide some reasons for its prima facie conclusion, especially in appealable cases.

application.fact_text: The Supreme Court clarified that to grant bail under such a statute, it must be satisfied that the alleged offences "cannot be held to be prima facie true."

To arrive at this conclusion, the court must perform at least a "surface-analysis of the probative value of the evidence." This may sometimes require the court to "probe into the matter deeper" to assess whether the collected materials would justify a conviction.

The Court emphasized that any findings recorded during the bail hearing are "tentative in nature." These preliminary findings will not have any bearing on the merits of the case during the actual trial.
The trial court remains free to decide the case based on the evidence presented at trial, without being prejudiced by the prima facie opinion formed at the bail stage.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that for the purpose of granting bail, the court is required to form a prima facie opinion based on the materials on record. To grant bail, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty (i.e., the accusation is not 'prima facie true'). This involves a surface-level analysis of the evidence's value. The Court affirmed that these findings are explicitly tentative and must not influence the subsequent trial on the merits.

arguments.issue_text: Whether, for the purpose of granting bail, the court is required to form a prima facie opinion based on the materials on record that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty, with such findings being tentative and not influencing the trial on merits.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that the court is obligated to conduct a prima facie review of the evidence on record to determine if there are reasonable grounds to believe the accusations are not true before deciding on bail. This assessment is a necessary prerequisite for granting bail under stringent statutes.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (prosecution) likely argued, citing the judgment in Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali, that the documents and evidence they rely upon at the bail stage should be considered to prevail until they are overcome or disproved by other evidence, suggesting a limited scope for the court's prima facie assessment.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb
cases.principle: A bail restricting clause cannot denude the jurisdiction of a Constitutional Court to grant bail under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.

cases.case_name: Angela Harish Sontakke v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: A bail restricting clause cannot denude the jurisdiction of a Constitutional Court to grant bail under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The interpretation of the word “terrorist” within a statute is to be related to the meaning of the same expression as used in Section 15 of that Act.
obiter: It is one of the basic rules of statutory construction that an expression used in different parts of a statute shall ordinarily convey the same meaning, unless a contrary intention appears from different parts of the same enactment itself.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that providing a prima facie assessment of the evidence is a mandatory requirement for a court deciding a bail application, particularly when the order is appealable, as it allows the appellate court to understand the basis for the decision. The court stated: "We also feel that such expression of prima facie reasons for granting bail is a requirement of law in cases where such orders on bail application are appealable, more so because of the fact that the appellate court has every right to know the basis for granting the bail. Therefore, we are not in agreement with the argument addressed by the learned counsel for the accused that the High Court was not expected even to indicate a prima facie finding on all points urged before it while granting bail..."
legal_tests_applied: When deciding on bail, the court is "duty-bound to apply its mind to the allegations put forth by the investigating agency and ought to have given at least a prima facie finding in regard to these allegations because they go to the very root of the right of the accused to seek bail."

Under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, the court must "satisfy ourselves that the specified offences alleged to have been committed by the appellants cannot be held to be prima facie true."

A bail-restricting clause under a statute cannot override constitutional protections, as it "cannot denude the jurisdiction of a Constitutional Court in testing if continued detention in a given case would breach the concept of liberty enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution of India, would apply in a case where such a bail-restricting clause is being invoked on the basis of materials with prima facie low-probative value or quality."
policy_considerations: For the proper functioning of the justice system, trial courts must provide reasons for their bail decisions to enable effective appellate review: "the appellate court has every right to know the basis for granting the bail."

The fundamental right to liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution prevents prolonged pre-trial detention based on stringent bail clauses, especially when the evidence presented by the prosecution is weak: "a bail-restricting clause cannot denude the jurisdiction of a Constitutional Court in testing if continued detention in a given case would breach the concept of liberty enshrined in Article 21..."

Lengthy incarceration as an undertrial, in this case almost five years, coupled with weak evidence, militates against the continued denial of bail, as seriousness of the allegations alone is not a sufficient ground for denial: "considering the fact that almost five years have lapsed since they were taken into custody, the appellants have made out a case for granting bail. Allegations against them no doubt are serious, but for that reason alone bail cannot be denied to them."
